column4: The food-law passage explicitly makes severe hunger a state of compulsion and grants a merciful exception to one not inclining to sin, giving famine a concrete legal consequence.
God is identified as the One who feeds and is not fed, establishing the divine provision invoked both rightly by the fed city and evasively by those refusing to feed others.
Joseph asks to be placed over the land's storehouses because he is a knowledgeable guardian, supplying the human stewardship that carries stored food through the severe years.
Those who believe and do good mutually counsel truth and mutually counsel patience, directly repeating the communal stance of تَوَاصَوْا۟ بِٱلصَّبْرِ beside the section's counsel to mercy.
Concealed alms given to poor people are declared better for the giver, directly protecting aid to hidden need from becoming performance.
Within the dependent-property passage, vulnerable people are to be provided and clothed from the wealth that sustains life and addressed kindly, joining material care to merciful speech.
God asks no provision from creatures and does not ask them to feed Him, clarifying the asymmetry between the divine Provider and hungry human recipients.
God is the Provider possessed of firm power, completing 51:57's feeding claim without turning divine provision into an excuse for human withholding.
Every creature's provision is attributed to God together with knowledge of its dwelling and repository, closely joining sustenance to the place in which a creature can remain.
Moses and his companion ask a town's inhabitants for food, but the inhabitants refuse hospitality; settled people deny visiting hunger exactly where the section calls the city-dweller to meet it.
Towns exulting in their livelihood are destroyed and their dwellings left nearly uninhabited, joining h-l-k, settlement, and lost provision in one reversal.
Charity spoiled by reminders and injury is likened to dust on smooth rock stripped bare by rain, joining failed giving to a ground that cannot retain or produce sustenance.
The command forbids killing children because of present poverty and promises provision for adults and children, setting a firm boundary around treatment of dependents under scarcity.
The parallel command forbids killing children from fear of future poverty and promises their provision, refusing to let anticipated hunger erase mercy toward the vulnerable.
Barren earth stirs, swells, and grows after water descends, a direct productive reversal of the dry ground carried in the section's secondary h-l-k sense.
Humbled, lifeless-looking earth stirs and swells when rain reaches it, giving another exact boundary between drought-struck ground and restored life.
The question asks who could provide if God withheld His provision, making the hidden or withdrawn source of sustenance perceptible behind human confidence.
A visitation from the Lord circles the garden while its owners sleep, beginning the removal of the crop they intended to keep from the poor.
The garden becomes stripped bare, turning the owners' apparently secure abundance into the very deprivation they planned for the miskīn.
The owners recognize that they themselves have become deprived, a pointed reversal of their resolve to deprive the visiting poor person.
They confess that they transgressed, naming the moral character of the exclusion once its consequence reaches them.
They hope their Lord will replace the garden with something better and turn toward Him, placing repentance and renewed provision beyond the scene of withholding.
The narrative names this outcome a punishment and warns of the greater punishment to come, completing the consequence of barring the poor from the harvest.

The Israelites are told to descend to a town to obtain the varied foods they demand, a food-directed movement into settlement that contrasts with famine-driven entry and with gratitude for received provision.
Ordinarily forbidden foods become permitted to one compelled by necessity without desire or transgression, marking a concrete boundary that extreme hunger changes.
The food prohibitions again yield for a person compelled by necessity without willful transgression, showing mercy operating at hunger's limit.
The repeated food law exempts the compelled person and closes with divine forgiveness and mercy, a specific legal reversal produced by desperate need.
The garden owners swear that they will harvest in the morning, establishing the crop and confident plan that culminate in excluding the miskīn.
On seeing the altered garden, they first think they have lost their way, registering how completely the expected source of food has disappeared.
The most balanced among them recalls having warned the others to glorify God, locating their failure in the stance taken toward provision before the loss.
They glorify their Lord and acknowledge that they were wrongdoers, supplying the recognition that follows the garden's reversal.
Fear of failing justice toward orphan girls creates a protective legal boundary, another concrete answer to the neglect and overlooked good contained in the source account of yatīm.
People are asked to imagine leaving weak offspring behind and therefore to fear God and speak rightly, making care for future parentless dependents personal.
Mercy toward aging parents is expressed through lowered bearing, care, and prayer, a Quranic instance of raḥma generating conduct rather than remaining an inward feeling.
Those who ridicule voluntary givers and people able to contribute only their effort are condemned, protecting small acts of giving made under limited means.
Women are to be lodged where the addressee dwells according to his means and not harmed to constrain them, concretely joining s-k-n with material support for remaining in place.
Each person must spend according to what God has given, and ease is promised after hardship, defining provision under unequal and straitened means.
Water produces crops of varied colors before they wither, yellow, and become debris, tracing the precise passage from provision-bearing field to lost yield.
The condemned person amasses and repeatedly counts wealth, an inward-hoarding counterpart to the boast of having consumed much wealth without making mercy reach the needy.
He imagines that wealth will make him endure, exposing the false security behind keeping goods from the vulnerable people who need them now.
